first_pass_flagged.quote: So: no thinking ahead in sentences,
first_pass_flagged.evidence: Anthropic's interpretability study ("Tracing the thoughts of a large language model", 27 March 2025, on Claude 3.5 Haiku) found the opposite. It says the model writes one word at a time but plans ahead. When writing a rhyming couplet, it picked the rhyme word ("rabbit") before it started writing the line. When researchers removed that planned word, it rewrote the line to end in "habit". Anthropic sums this up as Claude planning what it will say "many words ahead". The team had expected to show that the model did not plan ahead. Separately, today's 'reasoning' chatbots (OpenAI o1 onward) are described as models that 'think before they answer', producing a long hidden chain of thought before the reply. Output still comes one piece at a time, but 'no thinking ahead' contradicts published research, and knowledgeable viewers would notice.
first_pass_flagged.fix: So: it can plan a little ahead inside, but it writes one piece at a time, and it doesn't look things up unless it's given a tool to do so.

first_pass_flagged.quote: A deductible is the part of a covered loss that you pay yourself before the insurance pays anything.
first_pass_flagged.evidence: This is the standard textbook definition. NAIC: 'A deductible is the amount of loss paid by the policyholder before any loss is paid by the insurer.' HealthCare.gov (archived): 'The amount you owe for health care services your health insurance or plan covers before your health insurance or plan begins to pay.' It holds for car and home policies. But the script later applies the word to health plans too, and there 'before the insurance pays anything' isn't true: HealthCare.gov says all Marketplace plans pay the full cost of certain preventive benefits before you meet your deductible, and many plans pay for things like check-ups (or charge only a copay) before it. The simplest fix is a short caveat in the health-plan line (see that claim), not a rewrite here.
first_pass_flagged.fix: Keep this sentence, and add the health-plan caveat to the Calendar section (wording given under "On many health plans, it adds up across a year.").

first_pass_flagged.quote: and there's usually no point in claiming.
first_pass_flagged.evidence: For a car or home repair under a per-claim deductible, there is nothing to collect, and consumer sources agree it usually isn't worth filing. Two cases where a knowledgeable viewer would object. (1) Car accidents: most policies require prompt notice of an accident whether or not you claim, and insurers can deny later coverage (for example, if the other driver claims against you) when you didn't report it. Sources separate 'filing a claim' from 'reporting'. (2) Health plans, which the video brings up next: a bill under the deductible still goes through the plan, so the negotiated rate applies and the amount counts toward the yearly deductible. Saying 'no point in claiming' without a qualifier could mislead on both.
first_pass_flagged.fix: That's under your deductible, so the insurer pays nothing, and for a repair like this there's usually no point in claiming. (After a car accident, though, your policy may still require you to report it.)

first_pass_flagged.quote: How to Read a Lease: The Six Parts
first_pass_flagged.evidence: 'The Six Parts' suggests leases have a standard six-part structure. They don't: there is no legal or industry standard division, and guides list a dozen or more common sections (parties, term, rent, security deposit, occupancy, use rules, maintenance and repairs, landlord entry, insurance, default and termination, indemnification, boilerplate), with state landlord-tenant law overriding some clauses. Picking six to focus on is fine; presenting them as 'the' six parts is not.

edits.quote: That's under your deductible, so the insurer pays nothing, and there's usually no point in claiming.
edits.replace_with: That's under your deductible, so the insurer pays nothing. On a car or home policy, there's usually no point in claiming, though after a car accident your policy may still require you to report it.
edits.reason: As written, this applies to every kind of policy. Two sections later the script says health-plan deductibles add up across a year. On those plans a $400 bill does matter: put through the plan, it gets the plan's negotiated rate and counts toward the yearly deductible. A viewer could take 'no point in claiming' as a reason to skip using their health insurance, which would cost them money. On car policies, the standard ISO personal auto policy (Part E, Duties After an Accident or Loss) makes prompt notice of 'how, when and where the accident or loss happened' a condition of coverage. Someone who stays silent after a small bump can lose coverage if the other driver claims later. 'Claiming' and 'reporting' are different things, and this line blurs them. The first checker's fix said 'a repair like this' and added a note in brackets. That doesn't name health plans and can't be read aloud cleanly. This version says which policies it means and gives the reporting point as a spoken clause.

edits.quote: On many health plans, it adds up across a year.
edits.replace_with: On many health plans, it adds up across a year, so smaller bills for covered care still count toward it, and some care, like a check-up, is often paid for by the plan before you reach it.
edits.reason: The script's definition says the deductible is paid 'before the insurance pays anything'. HealthCare.gov uses nearly the same wording, so the definition can stay. HealthCare.gov's own glossary then adds that many plans pay for some services, like a checkup, before the deductible is met, and that all Marketplace plans pay the full cost of certain preventive benefits even before it's met. Since the video applies the word to health plans, it should say so here. Saying small bills count toward the yearly deductible also explains why the $400 rule above doesn't carry over to health plans. The first checker's wording said check-ups are 'covered before you reach it'. In insurance terms all covered care is 'covered' before the deductible; the question is who pays. 'Paid for by the plan' is the precise version, so the fix doesn't add a new error.

edits.quote: How to Read a Lease: The Six Parts
edits.replace_with: How to Read a Lease: Six Parts to Check
edits.reason: 'The Six Parts' says leases have a fixed six-part structure. There's no legal or industry standard like that. Guides list a dozen or more usual sections (parties, term, rent, deposit, occupancy, use rules, repairs, landlord entry, insurance, default and termination, and so on), and state landlord-tenant law overrides some clauses. Choosing six to focus on is fine; calling them 'the' six parts isn't. I dropped 'First' from the first checker's version, because it would add a claim about what order to read a lease in.

missed_by_first_pass: The first checker's health-plan fix says check-ups are 'covered before you reach it'. In insurance terms every covered service is covered before the deductible; what changes is who pays. HealthCare.gov says plans 'pay for' those services before the deductible is met. Their wording would have added an inaccuracy an expert would notice.

Their fix for the $400 line ('for a repair like this', plus a note in brackets) still lets a viewer apply 'no point in claiming' to health bills, which the very next section says add up across the year. The note in brackets also can't be spoken naturally.

The difference between claiming and reporting has a primary basis, not just the consumer sites they cited: the standard ISO personal auto policy (Part E) makes prompt notice of any accident or loss a condition of coverage. Their supporting source (cheapinsurance.com) is weak.

In the $3,000 example the insurer pays everything above the deductible. That's right for a car or home repair, but on most health plans you keep paying coinsurance or copays after the deductible until you reach the out-of-pocket maximum. The script doesn't say otherwise, but the follow-up video ('one picture') mustn't reuse the $500/$2,500 split for a health bill.

'How much is the deductible?' can have more than one answer. Car policies often have separate collision and comprehensive deductibles. Home policies in storm areas often add a hurricane or wind deductible set as a percentage of the dwelling's insured value, which can be many thousands of dollars. This bears on the 'could I pay it tomorrow' question. It isn't wrong as written, so it's not an edit.
Not every health deductible is yearly: Medicare Part A's deductible applies per benefit period, which can happen more than once a year. The script's 'many' covers this.
Some of the first pass's citations aren't good enough to publish (cheapinsurance.com, a miscapitalised Wikipedia link). Keep them out of the description.
